documents.title: Maize production manual for smallholder farmers in Tanzania
documents.text: Maize is the most important food crop in Tanzania, grown mostly under rain-fed, low-input conditions. Good agricultural practices start with choosing a variety suited to the local agro-ecology and to the length of the rainy season. Test germination before planting and buy seed from a recognized source. Plant at the start of the reliable rains, at the recommended spacing for a sole crop, and thin or fill gaps early so that the final plant population is even. Intercropping or rotating maize with grain legumes such as cowpea, beans or groundnut helps restore soil fertility and gives extra food and income. Check soil fertility before the season, using a simple visual assessment or a soil test where available. Apply compost or

documents.title: Maize production manual for smallholder farmers in Tanzania
documents.text: Check soil fertility before the season, using a simple visual assessment or a soil test where available. Apply compost or animal manure, and use mineral fertilizer at the recommended rate, split between planting and top-dressing, so that nutrients are available when the crop needs them. Where soils are acid, agricultural lime may be needed. Weed early, because the first weeks after emergence are the most sensitive to competition. Scout fields regularly for maize stem borer, fall armyworm, termites and disease symptoms such as maize lethal necrosis. For fall armyworm, look for fresh whorl damage and larvae, and use integrated options: resistant or tolerant varieties, timely planting, intercropping, hand-picking where feasible, and approved biopesticides. Avoid spraying indiscriminately, since this kills natural

documents.title: Maize production manual for smallholder farmers in Tanzania
documents.text: resistant or tolerant varieties, timely planting, intercropping, hand-picking where feasible, and approved biopesticides. Avoid spraying indiscriminately, since this kills natural enemies and can be unsafe for the applicator. Harvest when grains are fully mature and dry the crop thoroughly before shelling. Store shelled grain in a clean, dry, well-ventilated store or sealed containers, keep it off the floor, and check regularly for insects and mould. Good drying and storage are the cheapest way to protect the harvest and the family's food supply.

documents.title: Integrated management of the Fall Armyworm on maize: a guide for Farmer Field Schools in Africa
documents.text: Fall armyworm is a major pest of maize across Africa and can also feed on many other plants. Farmers first learn to recognize it: moths lay egg masses on leaves, young larvae feed in the whorl and leave characteristic window-pane feeding marks and sawdust-like frass, while larger larvae hide in the whorl or between the ear and the stalk. Regular scouting from early vegetative growth onwards is the basis of management, because young larvae are much easier to control than large ones. The guide promotes integrated pest management rather than routine spraying. Promising options include using varieties that are less susceptible, planting at the right time, maintaining healthy and fertile soils, and increasing diversity on the farm. Intercropping maize with

documents.title: Integrated management of the Fall Armyworm on maize: a guide for Farmer Field Schools in Africa
documents.text: susceptible, planting at the right time, maintaining healthy and fertile soils, and increasing diversity on the farm. Intercropping maize with legumes and the push-pull system, in which a repellent plant such as Desmodium is intercropped and an attractive border crop such as Napier grass is planted around the field, reduce infestation and support natural enemies such as parasitic wasps, ants and birds. Mechanical and local controls include hand-picking and crushing egg masses and larvae where infestation is low, and the careful use of locally available materials such as ash, soil, sand, lime, soap, salt or oil, applied directly to the whorl. Botanical preparations made from locally available plants are described, but their preparation and dose need to be correct. Where

documents.title: Integrated management of the Fall Armyworm on maize: a guide for Farmer Field Schools in Africa
documents.text: whorl. Botanical preparations made from locally available plants are described, but their preparation and dose need to be correct. Where intervention is needed, biopesticides based on naturally occurring pathogens are preferred. If chemical pesticides are used, they must be approved, dosed correctly, and handled with protective equipment, observing the harvest interval. Farmer Field Schools are used to test these options side by side in the field, compare damaged and undamaged plants, count larvae, and keep records of costs and yields. Community-wide monitoring and data sharing make management more effective than acting on isolated farms.

documents.title: Save and Grow in practice: maize, rice, wheat
documents.text: Save and Grow is an ecosystem approach to farming that aims to produce more from the same land while conserving natural resources. For maize, rice and wheat, the guide recommends three mutually reinforcing practices: minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover with crop residues or cover crops, and diversification through rotations and associations. Together these practices rebuild soil organic matter, improve water infiltration and storage, reduce erosion, and lower labour costs over time. For maize-based systems, rotating with grain legumes supplies nitrogen and breaks pest and disease cycles. Residues should be retained on the field instead of burned, and planted directly through the mulch where possible. In rice, alternate wetting and drying can save water without reducing yield when it is

documents.title: Save and Grow in practice: maize, rice, wheat
documents.text: through the mulch where possible. In rice, alternate wetting and drying can save water without reducing yield when it is managed correctly, and integrating rice with fish or ducks can add income and help control pests. Wheat systems benefit from diversifying rotations and from using varieties suited to local heat and drought conditions. The guide stresses that intensification must be adapted to local conditions. Good seed of adapted varieties, precise placement of modest amounts of fertilizer, timely weeding, and attention to planting dates are as important as the conservation practices themselves. Compost, manure and legume residues can reduce the need for purchased inputs, but nutrient removal in harvested grain must be replaced to avoid mining the soil. Farmers are encouraged

documents.title: Save and Grow in practice: maize, rice, wheat
documents.text: for purchased inputs, but nutrient removal in harvested grain must be replaced to avoid mining the soil. Farmers are encouraged to experiment on small plots, observe results, and adapt practices with local extension services. The approach is especially relevant to smallholders facing rising input costs and more erratic rainfall, because it lowers risk, protects the soil, and can raise yields sustainably without depending on large purchases of agrochemicals.

documents.title: Cassava Farmer Field Schools: resource material for facilitators in sub-Saharan Africa
documents.text: Cassava is a staple food for millions of people in sub-Saharan Africa and can produce acceptable yields on poor soils with few purchased inputs. Farmer Field Schools help groups of farmers learn by doing: they set up small trials in their own fields, compare local and improved practices, observe pest and disease development through the season, and discuss the results in regular group meetings. The resource material covers the cassava crop cycle from selecting healthy planting material to harvest and processing. Farmers learn to choose stems from healthy, high-yielding plants, to cut and plant them correctly, and to space plants so that the canopy closes at the right time. They compare practices such as minimum tillage, mulching, intercropping with grain

documents.title: Cassava Farmer Field Schools: resource material for facilitators in sub-Saharan Africa
documents.text: so that the canopy closes at the right time. They compare practices such as minimum tillage, mulching, intercropping with grain legumes, and the use of compost or manure. Intercropping cassava with cowpea or maize can give an earlier harvest, reduce erosion, suppress weeds and spread the risk of crop failure. Field exercises focus on identifying cassava diseases such as cassava mosaic disease and cassava brown streak disease, recognizing the symptoms early, and using healthy planting material to limit spread. Participants also learn to identify major pests and beneficial organisms, to estimate yield, and to keep simple records of labour, inputs and harvest. The facilitator's guide emphasizes that the farmer, not the instructor, generates the knowledge: each season's observations are used

documents.title: Cassava Farmer Field Schools: resource material for facilitators in sub-Saharan Africa
documents.text: and harvest. The facilitator's guide emphasizes that the farmer, not the instructor, generates the knowledge: each season's observations are used to decide what to change in the next season. This makes recommendations locally appropriate and increases the likelihood that farmers will adopt practices that genuinely improve yields, food security and income in their own fields.

documents.title: Save and Grow: Cassava — a guide to sustainable production intensification
documents.text: Cassava gives low yields when soils are exhausted and fields are cleaned by burning. The Save and Grow approach shows how smallholders can raise yields while protecting the soil. Three practices are central: minimum or zero tillage, keeping the soil covered with mulch or cover crops, and diversifying the farm with intercrops and rotations. Planting cassava without tillage on degraded land may give lower yields in the first years, but as soil health recovers, untilled land can produce high yields at lower cost. Mulch and cover crops suppress weeds and improve soil structure. Cassava grown in association, sequence or rotation with other crops increases income per unit area and reduces the risk of total crop loss. Intercropping with grain legumes

documents.title: Save and Grow: Cassava — a guide to sustainable production intensification
documents.text: with other crops increases income per unit area and reduces the risk of total crop loss. Intercropping with grain legumes such as cowpea or groundnut provides extra food and nitrogen, while protective hedgerows reduce erosion. Rotating cassava with legumes and cereals helps restore soil fertility. Healthy planting material is essential. Stems should come from vigorous, disease-free plants, be cut correctly, and be stored and planted so that they do not dry out. Planting at the recommended spacing and at the right time for the local rainy season gives the crop a good start. Where soils are shallow or hard, ridges or mounds increase the volume of soil available to the roots. Balanced applications of mineral fertilizer, combined with manure, compost

documents.title: Save and Grow: Cassava — a guide to sustainable production intensification
documents.text: or mounds increase the volume of soil available to the roots. Balanced applications of mineral fertilizer, combined with manure, compost and crop residues, can raise yields substantially, but nutrients removed in the harvested roots must be replaced. Pests and diseases are best managed through resistant varieties, healthy planting material, biological control agents and good field hygiene rather than routine insecticide use. The guide is intended for extension workers and farmers who want to intensify cassava production without degrading the land.

documents.title: Growing cassava: a training manual from production to postharvest
documents.text: Cassava is often called a zero-input crop, but good yields still depend on choosing the right land, variety, spacing and planting time. The training manual explains that the zero-input method avoids fertilizers and herbicides and instead encourages biological activity in the soil. It works best on land with adequate organic matter. Practice minimum tillage on sandy soils to conserve organic matter and moisture and reduce erosion; on shallow or hard soils, make ridges or mounds so that each plant has more topsoil. Use improved varieties with the highest and most stable yield in the local area. Select healthy stems, cut them correctly and plant them at the recommended spacing and time. Keep the field weed-free during the first months, because

documents.title: Growing cassava: a training manual from production to postharvest
documents.text: them correctly and plant them at the recommended spacing and time. Keep the field weed-free during the first months, because young cassava suffers badly from weed competition; later, the canopy shades most weeds. Cassava/maize and cassava/legume intercrops make better use of land, reduce erosion and lower the risk of crop loss. Harvest roots when they have reached a suitable size and maturity, usually several months after planting depending on the variety. Lift them carefully to avoid damage, since cut or bruised roots deteriorate quickly. Remove the roots from the field promptly and avoid leaving them exposed to sun and rain. Fresh cassava roots have a very short shelf life and can begin to rot within a few days. Transport them

documents.title: Growing cassava: a training manual from production to postharvest
documents.text: Fresh cassava roots have a very short shelf life and can begin to rot within a few days. Transport them quickly to the market or processing site, keep them in a cool shaded place, and process them into dried chips, flour or other products if storage is needed. The manual describes simple processing operations, hygiene and drying practices that reduce losses and improve the quality and market value of cassava products for smallholder farmers and processors.

documents.title: Guide to cowpea production in West Africa
documents.text: Cowpea is a key grain legume in West Africa, providing protein-rich food, fodder and income. Yields are often low because of insect pests, diseases, the parasitic weed Striga, poor soils and intermittent drought. The guide, prepared by IITA and national partners for Nigeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, Ghana and Senegal, sets out the steps farmers can take to improve production. Select a well-drained sandy loam for a rain-fed crop, since cowpea does not tolerate waterlogging. Clear the land, prepare a fine seedbed, and use good-quality seed without damage holes or wrinkles. The planting date matters: photoperiod-sensitive varieties should be planted from mid-July to mid-August in West Africa so that flowering is not delayed by long days, while early, photoperiod-insensitive varieties

documents.title: Guide to cowpea production in West Africa
documents.text: from mid-July to mid-August in West Africa so that flowering is not delayed by long days, while early, photoperiod-insensitive varieties can be planted whenever rainfall is sufficient. Choose a variety suited to the zone, considering maturity, drought tolerance, Striga resistance and consumer preference for seed colour and size. Sow at the recommended spacing for sole crops, or about 75 cm between rows and 25 cm within rows for a cowpea-maize intercrop; plant cowpea about four to six weeks after the cereal. Apply fertilizer according to the guide and manage weeds early. The major constraints include fungal diseases, bacterial blight, viruses, pod-sucking bugs, flower thrips and storage weevils. Resistant varieties, timely planting, good field hygiene and carefully timed, approved spraying where

documents.title: Guide to cowpea production in West Africa
documents.text: pod-sucking bugs, flower thrips and storage weevils. Resistant varieties, timely planting, good field hygiene and carefully timed, approved spraying where necessary are all part of management. Harvest pods when they are mature but before they split in the field, dry the grain well, and store it in clean, dry containers to protect it from storage pests.

documents.title: Rice production manual
documents.text: This rice production manual, prepared by IITA and the Tanzania Agricultural Research Institute, is written for smallholder rice farmers and extension workers in Tanzania. It covers the whole crop cycle in nine modules: choosing a good variety, land preparation, seed preparation, planting, field management, the cropping calendar, and managing salt-affected, saline-sodic and calcareous soils. Start with a variety that is suited to the local environment and to farmers' preferences for taste and market price. Prepare the field by clearing, tilling and levelling it, and make bunds to hold water. Level land is important because it allows an even water depth, which improves weed control and makes harvesting easier. Select good seed, and consider pre-sprouting or priming seed to improve germination

documents.title: Rice production manual
documents.text: which improves weed control and makes harvesting easier. Select good seed, and consider pre-sprouting or priming seed to improve germination and establish the crop quickly. Rice can be established by direct sowing or by transplanting seedlings. Transplant at the right age and spacing, with the correct number of seedlings per hill. Water management is critical: keep the field flooded during establishment, but use alternate wetting and drying where appropriate to save water. The manual describes the field water tube, a simple device that tells the farmer when the water level has fallen far enough to re-irrigate. Weed early, since weeds compete strongly with young rice. A cropping calendar helps plan land preparation, planting, weeding, fertilizer application and harvest so that

documents.title: Rice production manual
documents.text: compete strongly with young rice. A cropping calendar helps plan land preparation, planting, weeding, fertilizer application and harvest so that farm operations are done on time. On problem soils, use the specific recommendations in the manual: improved drainage and amendments for saline or sodic soils, and appropriate nutrient management for calcareous soils. Dry the grain thoroughly before storage to avoid mould and loss.

documents.title: Guide sur la production du niébé en Afrique de l'Ouest
documents.text: Ce guide de l'IITA et de ses partenaires destiné aux producteurs d'Afrique de l'Ouest présente les étapes clés de la culture du niébé. Il s'adresse notamment aux agriculteurs du Burkina Faso, du Ghana, du Mali, du Niger, du Nigeria et du Sénégal. Le niébé est une légumineuse importante pour l'alimentation, le fourrage et les revenus, mais sa production est limitée par les insectes, les maladies, le Striga, la faible fertilité des sols et la sécheresse. Choisissez un sol bien drainé, de préférence sableux, pour une culture de saison des pluies. Travaillez le sol suffisamment profondément pour permettre à la racine principale de pénétrer, mais adoptez le minimum de labour sur les sols fragiles. Utilisez des semences saines, sans trous ni

documents.title: Guide sur la production du niébé en Afrique de l'Ouest
documents.text: principale de pénétrer, mais adoptez le minimum de labour sur les sols fragiles. Utilisez des semences saines, sans trous ni rides, et traitez-les avant le semis si nécessaire. La date de semis est déterminante : les variétés sensibles à la photopériode doivent être semées de mi-juillet à mi-août pour fleurir lorsque les jours raccourcissent, tandis que les variétés précoces insensibles à la photopériode peuvent être semées dès que la pluviométrie le permet. Choisissez une variété adaptée à votre zone, en tenant compte de la maturité, de la résistance à la sécheresse et au Striga, et des préférences des consommateurs. Semez à l'espacement recommandé, seul ou en association avec le maïs, le sorgho ou le mil. Faites un désherbage précoce et

documents.title: Guide sur la production du niébé en Afrique de l'Ouest
documents.text: à l'espacement recommandé, seul ou en association avec le maïs, le sorgho ou le mil. Faites un désherbage précoce et appliquez les engrais conseillés. Surveillez les principaux ravageurs : thrips, punaises suceuses des gousses, charançons du stockage, ainsi que les maladies fongiques, bactériennes et virales. Récoltez les gousses à maturité, séchez bien les grains et conservez-les dans des récipients propres et secs pour limiter les pertes après récolte.

documents.title: Guide to cowpea production in northern Nigeria
documents.text: Cowpea is widely grown in northern Nigeria, where it supplies food and fodder in the dry savannas. This IITA guide describes the practical steps for establishing and managing the crop under the conditions of the region. As in the rest of West Africa, success depends on using adapted varieties, planting at the right time and controlling the major pests and diseases. Choose a well-drained sandy or sandy-loam soil, because cowpea is sensitive to waterlogging. Clear and prepare the land early, and make ridges where this helps drainage or weed control. Select clean, healthy seed of a variety recommended for northern Nigeria, taking into account maturity period, drought tolerance, resistance to Striga and diseases, and the market preference for seed size

documents.title: Guide to cowpea production in northern Nigeria
documents.text: Nigeria, taking into account maturity period, drought tolerance, resistance to Striga and diseases, and the market preference for seed size and colour. Treat seed before sowing where recommended. Planting date affects both yield and the need for insect control. Where rainfall is limited, sow so that flowering and pod filling occur while moisture is still available. In the northern savannas, later planting can help avoid the heaviest pest pressure, but it must not expose the crop to drought at flowering. Sow at the recommended intra-row and inter-row spacing and depth; for intercrops with cereals, follow the arrangements given in the guide so that the cowpea receives enough light. Apply the recommended fertilizer, and weed during the early weeks. The main

documents.title: Guide to cowpea production in northern Nigeria
documents.text: guide so that the cowpea receives enough light. Apply the recommended fertilizer, and weed during the early weeks. The main insect problems are thrips before flowering, pod-sucking bugs during pod formation, and storage weevils after harvest. Diseases include fungal leaf spots, bacterial blight and viruses. Use resistant varieties, clean seed, field hygiene and approved control measures where needed. Harvest pods as they ripen, dry the seed thoroughly, and store it in clean, dry conditions to protect it from weevils and mould.

documents.title: Farmers' guide to increased productivity of improved legume-cereal cropping systems in the savannas of Nigeria
documents.text: This farmers' guide from IITA explains how to raise the productivity of legume-cereal cropping systems in the savannas of Nigeria. Rotations and intercrops of cowpea, soybean or groundnut with maize, sorghum or millet make better use of land and labour, improve soil fertility through nitrogen fixation, and reduce the build-up of pests and diseases that occur when the same crop is grown every year. Start by choosing the right combination for the farm. Where land is scarce, an intercrop gives two harvests from the same field; where land is more available, a rotation may be easier to manage. Use improved varieties of both crops that are suited to the local rainfall and soils. Prepare the land well and sow on

documents.title: Farmers' guide to increased productivity of improved legume-cereal cropping systems in the savannas of Nigeria
documents.text: varieties of both crops that are suited to the local rainfall and soils. Prepare the land well and sow on time, since a delay of even a week can reduce yield significantly. Follow the recommended row arrangements, plant populations and fertilizer rates for each crop, and apply phosphorus where soils are deficient. Weeding must be timely, especially during the first six weeks. The legume often covers the ground and suppresses later weeds, which reduces labour. Watch for major pests and diseases of both crops, including Striga, stem borers, foliar diseases and pod-sucking bugs. Where an intercrop is used, remember that spraying for one crop can affect the other, so choose products and timing carefully and follow all safety instructions. After

documents.title: Farmers' guide to increased productivity of improved legume-cereal cropping systems in the savannas of Nigeria
documents.text: spraying for one crop can affect the other, so choose products and timing carefully and follow all safety instructions. After harvest, return crop residues to the field where possible to build organic matter. Rotate the cereals with a legume at least every two or three seasons. Keep simple records of the yield of each component and of inputs used, so that the farmer can compare systems and decide which one gives the best return. The guide is intended for extension workers and farmers who want practical, locally tested options rather than a single fixed recommendation.

documents.title: Cowpea production: training manual (Manual Series No. 11)
documents.text: This IITA training manual gives an overview of cowpea production, from field selection to storage. Cowpea is grown across the tropics for its grain, leaves and fodder, and it fits well into rotations and intercrops because it fixes nitrogen. The manual is designed for training courses and extension work, so each stage is described in practical terms. Good seed is the first requirement. Use seed that is clean, well stored and free from insect damage, and test germination before sowing. Select a well-drained site: cowpea dislikes heavy, waterlogged soils. Prepare the land so that the taproot can penetrate, and sow at the correct depth and spacing. Planting date should be chosen so that flowering and pod filling avoid the worst

documents.title: Cowpea production: training manual (Manual Series No. 11)
documents.text: at the correct depth and spacing. Planting date should be chosen so that flowering and pod filling avoid the worst drought and, where photoperiod-sensitive varieties are used, so that flowering is not delayed by long days. Fertilizer requirements are modest but phosphorus is often needed; apply it at planting where soils are deficient. Keep the crop weed-free early, because cowpea is a poor competitor in its first weeks. The major insect pests attack flowers and pods, and several fungal, bacterial and viral diseases can reduce yield. Resistant varieties, timely planting, crop rotation and good field hygiene are the foundation of control. Where pesticides are justified, use only approved products at the correct dose and observe the interval before harvesting or

documents.title: Cowpea production: training manual (Manual Series No. 11)
documents.text: control. Where pesticides are justified, use only approved products at the correct dose and observe the interval before harvesting or grazing. Harvest when pods are mature, and avoid leaving them too long in the field where they may split or be attacked by insects. Dry the grain to a safe moisture level, thresh carefully, and store in clean, dry, sealed containers. Storage pests can destroy a harvest that was otherwise successful, so check stored grain regularly and keep stores dry and well ventilated.

documents.title: Cereal-legume intercropping and rotations in Eastern and Southern Africa: farmer's manual
documents.text: This CIMMYT farmer's manual describes how to grow maize, sorghum and millet in rotation or intercrop with legumes such as common beans, soybeans, groundnuts and cowpea in eastern and southern Africa. These cereals are the staple food of the region and the main source of dietary carbohydrate, but continuous sole cropping on the same land depletes soils and increases pest and disease problems. Rotations and intercrops increase productivity and improve food and nutrition security. A legume following a cereal leaves nitrogen in the soil and breaks the cycle of pests such as Striga and stem borers. An intercrop spreads the risk of crop failure: if the cereal suffers from drought, the legume may still yield, and vice versa. The manual

documents.title: Cereal-legume intercropping and rotations in Eastern and Southern Africa: farmer's manual
documents.text: risk of crop failure: if the cereal suffers from drought, the legume may still yield, and vice versa. The manual gives step-by-step guidance on choosing the species and variety, arranging rows, planting at the right time and density, and applying fertilizer and manure. Timeliness is repeatedly emphasized. Plant with the first effective rains, weed early, and top-dress when the crop is actively growing. In drier areas, reduced tillage and retention of residues conserve moisture. Where labour is limited, a relay crop planted into a standing cereal can make better use of the season. The guide draws on experiences from Ethiopia, Malawi and South Africa and on wider work in sub-Saharan Africa. It stresses that the recommendations are general: farmers should

documents.title: Cereal-legume intercropping and rotations in Eastern and Southern Africa: farmer's manual
documents.text: Malawi and South Africa and on wider work in sub-Saharan Africa. It stresses that the recommendations are general: farmers should adapt them to their own agro-ecology and consult local extension services for variety and input advice specific to their district. Keeping records of yields and costs helps farmers judge which intercrop or rotation works best on their own land.

documents.title: Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN): a technical manual for disease management
documents.text: Maize lethal necrosis is a serious viral disease of maize that has caused severe losses in East Africa. This CIMMYT technical manual brings together best practices for managing it, for countries where the disease is established and for high-risk countries that want to prevent its introduction. The disease results from the combination of two viruses, maize chlorotic mottle virus and a potyvirus such as sugarcane mosaic virus, and infected plants show mosaic patterns, stunting and rapid drying. Because the viruses are transmitted by insects and can also be spread through seed and contaminated equipment, management starts with healthy seed and clean field practices. The manual describes surveillance and sampling protocols, leaf and seed sampling methods, and diagnostic tests for the

documents.title: Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN): a technical manual for disease management
documents.text: clean field practices. The manual describes surveillance and sampling protocols, leaf and seed sampling methods, and diagnostic tests for the viruses. Quarantine and phytosanitary measures help prevent movement of infected material into new areas. Resistant or tolerant germplasm is the most durable control. The manual explains how varieties are screened under artificial inoculation at the Naivasha screening facility in Kenya, and how breeders select for resistance. For farmers, the practical advice is to obtain seed from reliable sources, avoid saving seed from diseased fields, remove and destroy infected plants early, and control insect vectors where recommended. Early warning and emergency plans are described for national programmes. Farmers and extension workers should report unusual symptoms quickly so that outbreaks can be

documents.title: Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN): a technical manual for disease management
documents.text: plans are described for national programmes. Farmers and extension workers should report unusual symptoms quickly so that outbreaks can be confirmed and contained. The manual also covers pathogen-free commercial seed production and standard operating procedures, because the seed system is a key part of preventing further spread. Local extension services should be consulted for the varieties currently recommended in a given area.

documents.title: Package-of-practices for profitable maize cultivation: a field manual
documents.text: This CIMMYT field manual sets out a package of practices for profitable maize cultivation. Maize can grow on many soil types, from loamy sand to heavy clay, but it performs best on well-drained soils with good organic matter, adequate water-holding capacity and near-neutral pH. Salt-affected soils should be avoided, and maize is very sensitive to waterlogging, so low-lying fields with poor drainage are unsuitable. Prolonged cold below about five degrees Celsius also harms the crop. Begin with good seed of a suitable variety and a well-prepared seedbed. Plant at the recommended time and spacing so that the stand is uniform, and fill gaps or thin excess plants early. Apply organic manure or compost, together with mineral fertilizer where affordable, placing

documents.title: Package-of-practices for profitable maize cultivation: a field manual
documents.text: and fill gaps or thin excess plants early. Apply organic manure or compost, together with mineral fertilizer where affordable, placing nutrients near the root zone so that the young crop can use them efficiently. Split nitrogen applications where possible to reduce losses. Keep the field free of weeds, especially during the first weeks, and watch for major insect pests such as stem borers, termites and fall armyworm. Scout regularly and intervene early using approved, integrated control options. Avoid unnecessary insecticide use, which can harm beneficial insects and contaminate the crop. Harvest when the grain is mature, then dry it to a safe moisture content before shelling. Store grain in a clean, dry, ventilated structure, protect it from insects and rodents,

documents.title: Package-of-practices for profitable maize cultivation: a field manual
documents.text: a safe moisture content before shelling. Store grain in a clean, dry, ventilated structure, protect it from insects and rodents, and inspect it regularly. The manual emphasizes that yield and profit come from combining several modest improvements — good seed, timely operations, balanced nutrients, pest control and safe storage — rather than from any single input.

documents.title: Sorghum- and millet-legume cropping systems
documents.text: Sorghum and millet are the staple cereals of many dry areas of Africa. They grow where maize often fails: millet is the most drought tolerant, then sorghum. This cropping guide, produced by the Africa Soil Health Consortium, shows extension workers and farmers how to combine these cereals with legumes such as cowpea, groundnut and soybean in intercrops or rotations. Average yields of sorghum and millet in Africa are only about one and 0.5 tonnes per hectare, but they can often be doubled with good seed and good management. Use improved varieties, plant on time at the recommended spacing, weed early, and apply organic matter and mineral fertilizer where possible. Soils in sorghum and millet areas are often poor and fallows

documents.title: Sorghum- and millet-legume cropping systems
documents.text: and apply organic matter and mineral fertilizer where possible. Soils in sorghum and millet areas are often poor and fallows are short, so integrated soil fertility management is essential. Sorghum responds better to improved soil conditions than millet. Intercropping with legumes improves yields, soil fertility and food security. Cowpea and groundnut are the most common partners; soybean is suited only to wetter zones with more than about 700 mm of rain per year. A cereal-legume intercrop should be planted in rows that make harvesting and weeding possible, and the legume should be given enough light. Rotations with legumes help control Striga and other pests. In the drier environments, minimum tillage and retention of crop residues conserve scarce moisture and reduce

documents.title: Sorghum- and millet-legume cropping systems
documents.text: Striga and other pests. In the drier environments, minimum tillage and retention of crop residues conserve scarce moisture and reduce erosion. Plant with the first reliable rains and thin seedlings to the correct population. Harvest the panicles when grain is mature, dry them thoroughly and store the grain in dry, clean conditions to prevent mould and insect damage. Local extension services should be consulted for the varieties and fertilizer rates recommended in each district.

documents.title: Groundnut cropping guide
documents.publisher: CABI / ICRISAT / Africa Soil Health Consortium
documents.text: Groundnut yields in Africa are often below one tonne per hectare, but the crop can reach two to three tonnes or more with good practices. This guide from the Africa Soil Health Consortium explains the requirements of groundnut and how to fit it into intercrops and rotations. Groundnut grows best in deep, loose, well-drained sandy or sandy-loam soils without compaction layers, because the pegs must enter the soil and the pods must be pulled out at harvest. Heavy clay soils and waterlogging are unsuitable. The soil should be light coloured and slightly acidic to neutral, with a pH around 5.5 to 7.0; groundnut does not tolerate saline soils. If a handful of moist soil can be rolled into a stable

documents.title: Groundnut cropping guide
documents.publisher: CABI / ICRISAT / Africa Soil Health Consortium
documents.text: to 7.0; groundnut does not tolerate saline soils. If a handful of moist soil can be rolled into a stable ribbon, the soil has too much clay. Prepare a deep seedbed, breaking any hardpan and incorporating crop residues into the top soil. Apply lime if the soil is acidic and phosphorus fertilizer before planting, since most African groundnut soils are phosphorus deficient. Plant at the recommended spacing on flat beds or ridges; ridges help where drainage is poor. Groundnut should not follow groundnut in successive seasons. Rotate it every two to five years with maize, sorghum or millet, which benefit from the nitrogen it fixes, and avoid rotations with soybean, tobacco, cotton or tomatoes because of soil-borne diseases. Water is

documents.title: Groundnut cropping guide
documents.publisher: CABI / ICRISAT / Africa Soil Health Consortium
documents.text: from the nitrogen it fixes, and avoid rotations with soybean, tobacco, cotton or tomatoes because of soil-borne diseases. Water is needed most during emergence and during flowering, pegging and pod development. Where rainfall is high, use ridges; where water is scarce, use tied ridges to conserve moisture. Keep the crop weed-free, watch for leaf spot diseases and nematodes, and harvest when the pods are mature. Dry the pods well before shelling and store the kernels in dry conditions to avoid mould and aflatoxin contamination.

documents.title: Guide for sustainable sorghum production in Ghana
documents.text: This IITA guide, produced with Ghana's Savannah Agricultural Research Institute, gives practical advice for sustainable sorghum production in Ghana. Sorghum is a drought-tolerant cereal grown mainly in the savannas, where it is used for food, feed and brewing. Yields are usually low because farmers use traditional varieties, plant late, weed late and apply few nutrients. Choose a variety recommended for the agro-ecological zone, based on maturity, yield potential, resistance to pests and diseases, tolerance of Striga and drought, and market or household preferences. Use good-quality seed and treat it where recommended. Prepare the land early and plant with the onset of the reliable rains, at the correct depth and spacing. Early planting lets the crop use the available moisture and

documents.title: Guide for sustainable sorghum production in Ghana
documents.text: of the reliable rains, at the correct depth and spacing. Early planting lets the crop use the available moisture and escape the worst pest pressure. Fertility management combines organic and mineral sources. Apply compost or manure, and use fertilizer at the recommended rate, placing it near the plants. Where soils are acid, lime may be needed. Weed during the first weeks after emergence; late weeding causes large yield losses. Sorghum can be intercropped or rotated with legumes such as cowpea, soybean or groundnut to improve soil fertility and diversify the harvest. Important pests and diseases include stem borers, aphids, grain mould, leaf diseases and the parasitic weed Striga. Use resistant varieties, good crop hygiene and approved control measures where necessary.

documents.title: Guide for sustainable sorghum production in Ghana
documents.text: mould, leaf diseases and the parasitic weed Striga. Use resistant varieties, good crop hygiene and approved control measures where necessary. Harvest when the grain is mature, dry the panicles thoroughly, and store the threshed grain in clean, dry containers. Consult local extension officers for the varieties and recommendations appropriate to a specific district, since conditions differ across Ghana's sorghum-growing areas.

documents.title: Save and Grow: a technical guide to agricultural practices in Zambia
documents.text: This FAO technical guide describes conservation agriculture and sustainable intensification practices for small-scale farmers in Zambia. It focuses on maize-based systems, often combined with grain legumes such as pigeon pea, and on the services and markets farmers need to adopt these practices. The core principles are minimum soil disturbance, maintaining a permanent soil cover and diversifying crop species. Instead of ploughing every season, farmers open small planting basins or use direct seeding, leaving crop residues on the surface. The residues protect the soil from erosion, reduce evaporation and gradually build organic matter. Over time, this improves soil structure and water infiltration, which matters in seasons with erratic rainfall. Rotations and associations with legumes, especially pigeon pea, supply nitrogen and give

documents.title: Save and Grow: a technical guide to agricultural practices in Zambia
documents.text: infiltration, which matters in seasons with erratic rainfall. Rotations and associations with legumes, especially pigeon pea, supply nitrogen and give farmers an additional food and income source. The guide gives practical details on choosing adapted seed, deciding planting dates and spacing, managing weeds without a plough, and applying fertilizer precisely where it is needed. Fire should be kept off the field, since burning residues destroys the soil cover. Beyond the field, the guide discusses mechanization services, better links to agri-business hubs and access to markets. Smallholders often lack equipment and credit, so shared services and farmer organizations can make conservation farming practical. Farmers are encouraged to start on a small area, compare yields and labour with their usual practice, and

documents.title: Save and Grow: a technical guide to agricultural practices in Zambia
documents.text: farming practical. Farmers are encouraged to start on a small area, compare yields and labour with their usual practice, and adapt the system with local extension advice before expanding it to the whole farm.

documents.title: Sustainable intensification of cassava cropping systems
documents.text: This study from IITA and partners, conducted in Malawi, looks at how to improve cassava yields, soil health, incomes and climate resilience on small farms. Farmland is shrinking, soils are depleted, few crops are grown and suitable varieties are often unavailable. Researchers tested different nutrient combinations and intercropping arrangements, especially alternating rows of cassava and cowpea, across three agro-ecological zones and later on farmers' fields in seven districts. The most promising treatment was cassava intercropped with cowpea variety Sudan 1 in alternating single rows, with 60 kg of nitrogen per hectare for cassava split into two applications and 30 kg of nitrogen per hectare for cowpea. This system gave higher grain and storage-root yields, better land-use efficiency and greater profitability

documents.title: Sustainable intensification of cassava cropping systems
documents.text: of nitrogen per hectare for cowpea. This system gave higher grain and storage-root yields, better land-use efficiency and greater profitability than farmers' traditional practice. Sudan 1 also out-yielded the alternative cowpea variety IT82E-16, showing that variety choice matters in an intercrop. The practical message for farmers is that cassava and cowpea can be grown together successfully when the rows are arranged properly, the varieties are well matched and nutrients are applied in modest, split doses placed where the roots can use them. Intercropping diversifies the harvest, gives an earlier grain crop and helps restore soil health through the legume. The technology was approved for release by Malawi's Agricultural Technology Clearing Committee. As with any recommendation, farmers should check which varieties

documents.title: Sustainable intensification of cassava cropping systems
documents.text: technology was approved for release by Malawi's Agricultural Technology Clearing Committee. As with any recommendation, farmers should check which varieties and fertilizer rates are currently advised for their own area, since results depend on local soils and rainfall. Local extension services can provide that detail.

documents.title: Growing cassava in Nigeria
documents.text: Growing cassava in Nigeria is a practical IITA manual for farmers and extension workers. Cassava is one of the most important staple crops in Nigeria and much of West Africa, and it can be grown on a small scale with limited inputs. This guide describes the basic steps needed to obtain a good harvest. Start with healthy planting material. Use stem cuttings from vigorous plants that show no symptoms of mosaic disease or other problems, and take the cuttings from a healthy stem of the right age. Prepare the land properly: clear weeds, make ridges or mounds where the soil is heavy or shallow, and plant at the recommended spacing so that plants do not compete excessively. Plant at the

documents.title: Growing cassava in Nigeria
documents.text: is heavy or shallow, and plant at the recommended spacing so that plants do not compete excessively. Plant at the beginning of the rainy season so that the crop establishes with adequate moisture. Weed the field during the early months, since cassava is sensitive to weed competition before the canopy closes. Avoid damaging the stems during weeding. Where practical, intercrop with a short-duration legume such as cowpea to get an early harvest and help suppress weeds. Watch for cassava mosaic disease and cassava brown streak disease; remove infected plants and always use clean planting material, since these diseases are spread through stems and by whiteflies. Cassava roots are normally harvested several months after planting, depending on the variety. Dig them

documents.title: Growing cassava in Nigeria
documents.text: through stems and by whiteflies. Cassava roots are normally harvested several months after planting, depending on the variety. Dig them up carefully to avoid cuts and bruises, because damaged roots rot quickly. Fresh roots do not store for long, so either take them to market promptly or process them into gari, flour, chips or other products. Dry products store much longer and can be sold when prices are better, giving farmers more control over income.

documents.title: Climate smart agricultural technologies for the Sahel and Horn of Africa
documents.text: This technical report from the Technologies for African Agricultural Transformation programme reviews climate-smart agricultural technologies for the Sahel and the Horn of Africa. The region faces low and erratic rainfall, high temperatures, degraded soils and frequent droughts. The report collects practical options that help farmers produce more while adapting to climate change and, where possible, reducing emissions. The technologies include drought-tolerant and early-maturing varieties of sorghum, millet, maize and groundnut; soil and water conservation measures such as tied ridges, zai pits and mulching; small-scale irrigation and water harvesting; and integrated soil fertility management that combines manure, compost and modest amounts of mineral fertilizer. Micro-dosing, or placing a small quantity of fertilizer close to the seed, is highlighted as a way

documents.title: Climate smart agricultural technologies for the Sahel and Horn of Africa
documents.text: of mineral fertilizer. Micro-dosing, or placing a small quantity of fertilizer close to the seed, is highlighted as a way to raise yields with limited cash and thin soils. Intercropping cereals with legumes such as cowpea and groundnut improves soil fertility, diversifies the diet and reduces the risk of total crop failure. Groundnut, for example, grows well in rotation with cereals on lighter soils and needs calcium as well as phosphorus and potassium for pod development. Agroforestry and the use of crop residues help restore organic matter and protect fields from wind and erosion. The report stresses that no single technology works everywhere. Farmers should choose options that fit their rainfall zone, soils, labour and access to markets, and should

documents.title: Climate smart agricultural technologies for the Sahel and Horn of Africa
documents.text: technology works everywhere. Farmers should choose options that fit their rainfall zone, soils, labour and access to markets, and should test them on a small plot before adopting them widely. National extension services and research institutes are the right source of locally adapted varieties and input recommendations.

documents.title: Save and grow: a policymaker's guide to the sustainable intensification of smallholder crop production
documents.text: This FAO policymaker's guide explains why smallholder crop production must be intensified in an environmentally sustainable way. Food demand is rising, but nearly all additional production in the future must come from existing farmland, much of it already degraded. Continuing to expand into forests and marginal land is not a viable option. The guide sets out the principles of sustainable intensification: produce more from the same area while enhancing natural capital and ecosystem services. In practice this means combining better varieties, water management, soil fertility management and pest management, and reducing waste along the value chain. Conservation agriculture — minimum tillage, permanent soil cover and crop diversification — is one important component, but it must be adapted to local farming

documents.title: Save and grow: a policymaker's guide to the sustainable intensification of smallholder crop production
documents.text: tillage, permanent soil cover and crop diversification — is one important component, but it must be adapted to local farming systems rather than applied as a fixed package. Smallholders need support to intensify: access to good seed, fertilizer and equipment, credit, extension advice, reliable markets and secure land rights. Women and young people are often the main contributors to farm labour and need to be included in these services. The guide also emphasizes that higher yields alone do not guarantee better nutrition or incomes; diversification, value addition and market access matter too. For the purpose of this knowledge base, the relevant message is that advice to farmers should promote practices that raise productivity without exhausting the soil, and should be

documents.title: Save and grow: a policymaker's guide to the sustainable intensification of smallholder crop production
documents.text: relevant message is that advice to farmers should promote practices that raise productivity without exhausting the soil, and should be adapted to local conditions through farmer participation and good extension services. General recommendations from this guide should always be combined with locally specific advice on varieties, planting dates and input rates.

documents.title: Household water treatment and safe storage
documents.text: Household water treatment and safe storage (HWTS) improve the quality of drinking water and reduce diarrhoeal disease, especially for people who rely on unimproved water sources or on supplies that are not always safe. This is particularly important in emergencies, when normal water services may be disrupted. WHO explains that treatment is only one part of the solution. Water that has been treated can easily become contaminated again during transport and storage, so the treated water must be kept in a clean, covered container, and water should be drawn with a clean cup or tap rather than by dipping hands or dirty vessels into it. Storage containers should have a narrow mouth or a tap, and they should be cleaned

documents.title: Household water treatment and safe storage
documents.text: or dirty vessels into it. Storage containers should have a narrow mouth or a tap, and they should be cleaned regularly. Diarrhoeal disease can be caused by bacteria, viruses and parasites in water contaminated by faeces. Treatment methods that remove or inactivate these pathogens include boiling, chlorination, filtration and solar disinfection, depending on local conditions and on the quality of the source water. The effectiveness of a method depends on correct and consistent use, so households need clear instructions and reliable access to the product or fuel required. Covering water storage containers also reduces mosquito breeding, which can lower the risk of diseases such as dengue and malaria. HWTS is most useful where the safety of the water supply is

documents.title: Household water treatment and safe storage
documents.text: risk of diseases such as dengue and malaria. HWTS is most useful where the safety of the water supply is uncertain and where people are vulnerable, including young children and people with weakened immunity. It does not replace the need for safely managed water services, but it is a practical additional barrier against disease. For advice about a specific illness or outbreak, contact a local health professional or public health authority.

documents.title: Drinking-water fact sheet
documents.text: This WHO fact sheet summarizes why safe drinking water matters. Contaminated water can transmit diseases such as diarrhoea, cholera, dysentery, typhoid and polio, and unsafe water is responsible for a large number of diarrhoeal deaths each year. Access to a safely managed drinking-water service — water that is available, accessible and free from contamination — remains a major global challenge, including in the African Region. Households can reduce risk by protecting the source, treating water where its safety is uncertain and storing it safely. Storage containers should be covered to keep out dust, insects and faecal contamination, and clean water should be drawn with a clean vessel or tap. Standing water in and around the home can provide breeding sites

documents.title: Drinking-water fact sheet
documents.text: should be drawn with a clean vessel or tap. Standing water in and around the home can provide breeding sites for mosquitoes that transmit malaria, dengue and other diseases, so containers should be emptied, cleaned or covered. Water scarcity affects many communities and is worsening with population growth, urbanization andchanging rainfall patterns. When water is scarce, households may store more water in the home, which increases the risk of contamination if containers are not cleaned and covered. Water safety plans, used by utilities and communities, identify risks from the catchment to the tap and help prevent contamination before it happens. WHO monitors drinking-water quality and supports countries in testing household water treatment technologies against health-based performance criteria. People who suspect

documents.title: Drinking-water fact sheet
documents.text: WHO monitors drinking-water quality and supports countries in testing household water treatment technologies against health-based performance criteria. People who suspect that their water is unsafe, or who have symptoms such as persistent diarrhoea, should contact their local health provider or public health authority for advice specific to their situation.
